newsitem.title: UK: Hague fancied in race for UK Tory leadership.
newsitem.headline: Hague fancied in race for UK Tory leadership.

text.p: Former Welsh secretary William Hague emerged as favourite to take over the leadership of Britain's main opposition Conservative party on Wednesday after two "Eurosceptic" contenders pulled out of the contest and swung behind him.

But his two remaining rivals, former finance minister Kenneth Clarke and right-winger John Redwood, pledged to fight on and warned the battle to succeed former prime minister John Major was not over yet.
Major stood down immediately after his party's heavy election defeat by Tony Blair's Labour Party on May 1.

Clarke topped Tuesday's first round ballot with the backing of 49 of the 164 Conservative members of parliament -- the only people entitled to choose the party's leader -- with Hague in second place with 41 votes. Redwood trailed with 27.

But Hague, aged just 36, leapt into pole position for the second round ballot next Tuesday after former social security secretary Peter Lilley, who won 24 votes, and former home secretary Michael Howard, who took 23, threw their support behind him.
To win in the second ballot, a candidate needs the votes of more than half the 164 Conservative MPs. If there is no winner, the two front-runners slug it out two days later.

Redwood, who quit the cabinet in June 1995 to mount an unsuccessful challenge to Major's leadership, had expected Lilley and Howard to back him to unite right-wingers who are against increasing links with the European Union.
Clearly irritated, he said on Wednesday he had expected to win their support despite having no formal deal.

But Redwood dismissed suggestions that his campaign was now doomed. "I haven't talked about betrayal. There was no formal deal, but there were clear statements from the other two camps that they felt we should all get together after the ballot...

"It is a three-horse race for a bit and it will be a two-horse race at the end, and the media are getting it wrong consistently in trying to predict in advance," Redwood, Welsh secretary before he resigned and Hague took over, told the BBC.
Clarke warned that the party must unite to rebuild after its election mauling by Labour, which ended 18 years of unbroken Conservative rule.

"If the Conservative parliamentary party falls back to factional fighting and decides internal arguments of this kind are more important than the obvious view of the public, I think it will take us much longer to recover than it otherwise should."
Clarke is hoping the 164 Conservative MPs in the 659-seat parliament will take note of his overwhelming support from senior party activists in a consultative poll on Tuesday.
But party activists -- much to their anger -- have no say in choosing the leader and Clarke's pro-European views mean he has an uphill task winning right-wing support in the second round.
Probably the party's most effective parliamentary performer, Clarke sought to woo the right.

"If people are worried about the fact that they think I'm more on the left than any of the others that remain in (the race), well, I shall have to make sure that I put together a team that reflects the broad balance of the party," he said.
But it was Hague who was tipped for the leadership by newspapers and by punters.
Bookmakers William Hill quoted Hague at 4-5. Clarke was given odds of 11-10 and John Redwood 7-1.
